This aligns with a cautiously favorable (leans_endorse) evaluation.

report:
**Conclusion:** A qualified **yes**—for children **aged ≥12 months** with an uncomplicated acute cough (usually from a cold), honey can modestly reduce cough frequency/severity and improve sleep, especially overnight. It is symptom relief, not a cure for the infection.

The best synthesis (Cochrane) found honey probably outperformed placebo/no treatment on caregiver-rated cough frequency (two studies, 154 children; mean difference about 1 point on a 7-point scale). NICE likewise reports roughly 0.5–2-point improvements after one day. These are meaningful to some families but are based largely on short-term, subjective parent ratings—not evidence that honey shortens illness or prevents complications.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007094_honey-acute-cough-children  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng120/chapter/summary-of-the-evidence

**Why the conclusion is not stronger:** trials are small, heterogeneous, and often assess only a single night. A 2023 systematic review judged the overall evidence *low quality*; it also identified a 2022 randomized study finding no pharmacological effect on nocturnal cough or sleep. Honey has not consistently beaten dextromethorphan, although OTC cough medicines have their own limited benefits and potential harms in young children.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37355498/

**Safety:** Never give honey (including in drinks or cough mixtures) to infants under 12 months because of botulism risk. Seek medical advice promptly for breathing difficulty, dehydration, bluish color, unusual sleepiness, or a worsening/persistent cough.  
https://www.cdc.gov/infant-toddler-nutrition/foods-and-drinks/foods-and-drinks-to-avoid-or-limit.html
